nameStory: Catinaria atropurpurea gets its mysterious name from its distinctive dark purple-black reproductive structures called apothecia. The word 'atropurpurea' combines Latin 'atro' meaning dark or black with 'purpurea' for purple, perfectly describing the dramatic color that gives this lichen its most striking feature.
description: **[Uncertain - very limited information available]** Catinaria atropurpurea is a crustose lichen that forms thin, crusty patches on its host surface. Like other members of its family, it likely appears as a grayish to whitish crust when dry, but its most distinctive feature is its dark purple-black apothecia (reproductive structures) that look like tiny dark cups or discs scattered across the surface. This species appears to be extremely rare in New England, with only one recorded observation in our region.

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Look for distinctive dark purple-black apothecia that appear as small, cup-like or disc-shaped structures on the surface - these are the lichen's most diagnostic feature and stand out dramatically against the lighter crust

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms a thin, crusty coating that adheres tightly to the substrate and cannot be easily peeled away - feels rough and granular to the touch

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: The main body appears grayish-white to pale when dry, potentially darkening when wet, but always contrasted by the striking dark purple-black reproductive structures

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual patches may be small to moderate in size, with the dark apothecia measuring just a few millimeters across but clearly visible to the naked eye

habitat: **[Uncertain]** Based on its family relationships, this lichen likely grows on bark of trees or possibly rock surfaces in coastal or near-coastal areas of New England. Given its extreme rarity in our region, it may prefer very specific microhabitats or environmental conditions that are uncommon in New England.

seasonality.spring: **[Uncertain]** Like all lichens, visible year-round with apothecia potentially more noticeable as they develop. The contrast between wet spring conditions and dry periods may make identification features more apparent.
seasonality.summer: **[Uncertain]** Dry summer conditions likely show the full color contrast between the pale thallus and dark apothecia most clearly, making this the best season for confident identification.
seasonality.fall: **[Uncertain]** Autumn moisture may cause color changes in the main body of the lichen, but the distinctive dark apothecia should remain the key identifying feature regardless of weather.
seasonality.winter: **[Uncertain]** Winter conditions may make the lichen appear darker overall when wet from snow and rain, but the characteristic purple-black apothecia should still be distinguishable.

funFact: This lichen is so rare in New England that it's been documented only once in our entire region - making any sighting a truly exceptional discovery that could contribute valuable information to our understanding of lichen distribution and ecology!
confusionNotes: **[Uncertain]** The dark purple-black apothecia are so distinctive that once you spot them, confusion with other species is unlikely. However, without the reproductive structures visible, the crusty growth form could be mistaken for many other crustose lichens - always look for those telltale dark cups or discs.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Catinaria comes from Latin meaning 'little basin' or 'small bowl,' referring to the cup-shaped reproductive structures that are characteristic of this group. This lichen represents one of New England's rarest lichen species, highlighting how much we still have to learn about the cryptic world of crusty lichens.
compareHints: **[Uncertain]** Since this is the only Catinaria species recorded in New England, compare it with other members of the Ramalinaceae family that have dark apothecia. However, the specific purple-black color of the reproductive structures should distinguish it from related species, which typically have brown, black, or differently colored apothecia without the distinctive purple tint.
